subsection: 1. Economic indicators and their impact on business

notes.b: An economic indicator is a measure of how the economy is performing. Businesses read indicators to decide when to hire, borrow, invest, set prices or hold back, so they are the starting point for planning growth.
points: Indicators are published regularly by bodies such as the Central Statistics Office (CSO, Ireland's official statistics agency) and the European Central Bank (ECB), so a business can track trends over time rather than guess.
A business cannot control an indicator, but it can plan for it, for example by adjusting prices, staffing, borrowing and expansion before a change hits its costs or sales.
Every effect of an indicator comes back to a business's costs (what it pays to operate), revenue (what it earns from sales) and profit (revenue minus costs).
The other idea behind the effects is demand (how much customers want to buy at a given price). Exports (goods and services sold abroad) and imports (those bought from abroad) matter too.

Indicators should be read together, because a rise in one can offset or amplify the effect of another. For example, rising growth lifts demand, but if inflation is rising too, the business's costs are climbing at the same time.
notes.tip: When a question asks about the impact of an indicator, always link it to a specific cost or revenue effect, and remember that a change can help one business and hurt another, such as an exporter versus an importer.

notes.b: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, which means money buys less over time. It is not the same as one price going up: it is prices rising across the economy.
points: In Ireland the CSO measures inflation through the Consumer Price Index (CPI), which follows the cost of a fixed basket of goods and services bought by households and compares it with a base period. This is why it shows the average change in prices rather than any single price.

As of October 2026 the CSO reported that prices rose 4.3% in the 12 months to October 2026, up from 4.1% in September and the highest rate since December 2023. Housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels rose 10.7% and transport rose 9.0%.
Rising inflation raises a business's input costs, such as energy, materials and wages, and squeezes profit margins if the business cannot pass those costs on to customers.
Inflation erodes consumers' purchasing power (what their income can buy), so households cut back on non-essential spending, which reduces demand for many businesses.

Businesses respond by raising prices, renegotiating supplier contracts or finding cheaper inputs. How much they can raise prices depends on the level of competition they face, because customers will switch to a rival if one firm charges much more.

Ethical angle: rising prices fall hardest on lower-income households and on firms with little pricing power. An ethical business does not exploit a price spike to overcharge, and treats staff fairly when its own costs rise.
Digital angle: firms use digital tools to track their costs and prices and to change prices quickly when inflation moves.
notes.tip: Don't confuse inflation (the general price level rising) with a rise in a single price. In an explain question, give the mechanism (costs up, demand down) and then the effect on the business's growth.

notes.b: Employment indicators show how many people are working and how easily a business can find staff. They affect both sides of a business: who it can hire, and who can afford to buy from it.
points: The employment rate is the share of the working-age population in paid work. The unemployment rate is the share of the labour force without work who are available for work and actively seeking it. These are different shares of different groups, so do not mix them up.
The labour force is the people in work plus the people who are unemployed and seeking work. This is why the unemployment rate is measured against the labour force, not the whole population.

In Ireland the CSO publishes these figures from the Labour Force Survey, which is a household survey. In Quarter 3 2026 it counted 2,884,100 people in employment and 150,700 unemployed, a labour force of 3,034,800.
Low unemployment means more consumers have income to spend, so demand for goods and services tends to grow.

Low unemployment also makes it harder and more expensive to recruit, because workers have more choice of employer. This pushes up wages and can limit the expansion of labour-intensive firms (firms that rely on many staff, such as a hotel).
High unemployment reduces consumer spending and weakens demand, although it may let firms hire staff more easily and at lower cost.
notes.tip: Keep the two rates apart: employment rate is a share of the working-age population, unemployment rate is a share of the labour force. Show that low unemployment is good for demand but bad for recruitment costs.

notes.b: An interest rate is the cost of borrowing, a percentage of the amount borrowed, or the return paid on savings. It affects investment decisions in every business, because most expansion is paid for partly with borrowed money.
points: Ireland uses the euro, so the European Central Bank sets the main euro-area policy interest rates, and Irish banks set their own lending rates in response. The ECB does not set Irish bank loan or mortgage rates directly.
Higher interest rates raise repayments on variable-rate loans (loans whose rate moves with market rates) and overdrafts, which reduces business investment and household spending on credit.
Higher rates also make saving more attractive, which can reduce spending and the demand for borrowing.
Lower interest rates make borrowing cheaper, which encourages investment in equipment, premises and expansion, and supports consumer spending on credit.
A business with heavy debt is especially exposed to rate rises, so understanding the terms of its loans, including whether the rate is fixed or variable, is part of sound financial management.
notes.tip: If a question asks who sets interest rates, the answer is the European Central Bank. Common wrong answers are the Central Bank of Ireland, the government or the CSO.

notes.b: Economic growth and development are related but different, and both matter to business. Growth is about how much is produced; development is about how well people live.
points: Economic growth is an increase in the real value of goods and services produced over time, meaning the increase after allowing for inflation. Allowing for inflation matters because output can look larger simply because prices rose.
Gross domestic product (GDP) measures the value of output produced within a country's borders in a given period.
Gross national product (GNP) adjusts GDP by adding income earned abroad by residents and subtracting income paid to foreign owners.
Modified GNI, known as GNI*, is designed to remove distortions caused by the activity of multinational companies, so it gives a clearer view of the domestic economy in Ireland.

Ireland uses GNI* because GDP can overstate the size of the domestic economy when multinational activity is large. The CSO's figures for 2025 (preliminary) show GDP at 602,441 million euro against GNI* at 333,971 million euro, a big gap.
Growth affects business by increasing demand, which encourages expansion, new investment and hiring.

Economic development is broader than growth and includes improvements in living standards, health, education, environmental protection and social equality. A country can grow without developing if the gains are not shared or the environment suffers.

Development matters to business because it improves the skills base, infrastructure and social stability, which make a country more attractive for sustainable investment (investment that lasts without damaging people or the environment). The environmental and equality parts of development are the sustainability link.
notes.tip: Don't say GDP shows how well off Irish people are, because multinational activity inflates Irish GDP, which is why GNI* exists. Exams ask for growth versus development, so give output on one side and living standards, health, education and equality on the other.

notes.b: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another, and it affects any business that buys or sells across borders. Whether a change helps or hurts depends on whether the firm mainly exports or imports.
points: A stronger euro makes Irish exports more expensive for overseas buyers and imports cheaper, which can reduce the competitiveness of exporters.
A weaker euro makes Irish exports cheaper abroad, which helps exporters, but it raises the euro cost of imported raw materials and fuel.

Businesses earning revenue in dollars or sterling face currency risk, because a change in the exchange rate changes the euro value of that revenue, and they may hedge (take steps to protect themselves) against it.
Tourism businesses are affected too: a weaker euro can make Ireland cheaper for visitors from the United States or the United Kingdom, so a hotel may see more overseas bookings.
notes.tip: Never say a weaker euro is always good or a strong euro always bad. Say who it helps and who it hurts: an exporter of food products gains from a weaker euro, while an importer of materials pays more.

notes.b: Consumer confidence is how optimistic households feel about their own finances and the wider economy, and it is measured through regular surveys. It matters because confident households spend and worried ones hold back.
points: High confidence encourages spending on discretionary items (things people want rather than need) such as holidays, cars and dining out, which boosts retail, hospitality and tourism.
Low confidence leads households to save more and defer purchases, which hits businesses selling non-essential goods hardest.

Businesses respond to changes in confidence by adjusting stock levels, hiring plans and marketing budgets, often before the change shows in sales figures, because the survey signals what customers are likely to do.

A monthly consumer sentiment survey of 1,000 adults, reported on 3 November 2026, put confidence for October 2026 at 61.6. That was above its average since March of 59.6 but well below its 30-year average of 83.
notes.tip: Link confidence to the type of business: discretionary sellers such as a hotel or a car dealer feel a fall first, while sellers of essentials are less affected.

notes.h: Reading an indicator from a graph
notes.b: Exam questions often show an indicator as a graph or infographic, and the skill is to describe what it shows and then link it to business. Indicators are published as open data by the CSO and ECB, so the same skill applies to the digital dashboards and infographics firms use.
points: 1. Start by reading the title, the units, the scale and the time period, so that the indicator and its measurement are clear.
2. Identify the direction and rate of change, and any turning points, because a sudden change can matter more than a gradual one.
3. Quote figures from the graph accurately, and avoid treating a single data point as proof of a long-term trend.
4. Link the trend to business effects, such as rising costs or falling demand, and state what the business should do in response.
notes.tip: In an infographic question, name the indicator, say what it measures, read the trend (direction, size, time period) and then give the business impact. Common mistakes are naming the wrong indicator, ignoring the units, treating one data point as a trend and giving no business impact.

notes.h: Explaining the impact on a business's growth
notes.b: A strong answer picks indicators, then shows how each one changes a business's decision to grow. The same pattern works for any indicator.
points: For each indicator, state the direction of change, the mechanism (costs, demand, borrowing or exports) and the effect on the growth decision, such as whether to expand, hire or invest.
Tie each effect to a business type, for example a small retailer, an exporter of food products or a hotel, so the point is specific rather than general.
Pick effects that are really different from each other. If all three indicators lead to the same point, such as higher costs, the answer is thin.
For fuller discuss or evaluate answers, give positive and negative effects, say which business is affected most and why, and finish with a justified conclusion.
notes.tip: Common mistakes in explain answers are giving the definition only, giving a cause with no business effect, repeating the same effect for all three indicators, and leaving out the link to growth.

keyTerms.definition: A sustained rise in the general level of prices across the economy over time.
A measure of the average change in prices of a representative basket of goods and services bought by households.
The percentage of the working-age population who are in paid work.
The percentage of the labour force who are without work, available for work and actively seeking it.
The cost of borrowing money, expressed as a percentage of the amount borrowed, or the return earned on savings.
An increase in the real value of the goods and services produced in an economy over time.
The total value of goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given period.
The price of one currency in terms of another currency.
A measure of how optimistic households are about their own finances and the wider economy.

questions.prompt: Explain the impact of three economic indicators on the growth of a business of your choice.
questions.model: Choose a retailer or manufacturer. Inflation raises the cost of energy, materials and wages, so the business either raises prices, which may reduce sales, or absorbs the costs and earns less profit. Interest rates affect expansion, because a rise increases the cost of a bank loan for a new shop or factory and may delay growth plans, while a fall makes investment cheaper. Consumer confidence affects demand: when households feel secure they spend more on the business's products, so sales rise and the business can justify hiring staff and opening new locations.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between economic growth and economic development, and how each affects business.
questions.model: Economic growth is an increase in the real value of output over time, and it affects business mainly through higher demand, which encourages expansion and investment. Economic development is broader, covering living standards, health, education and social equality, and it affects business through a better-skilled workforce, improved infrastructure and social stability, which support sustainable growth. A business can benefit from growth in its sales, but it needs development to secure skilled staff and reliable markets over the long term.
